Stealth technology is crucial in modern defense systems.
Radar Cross-Section (RCS) is a numerical representation of an object's visibility relative to the radar system.
Geometric shaping is an effective method for RCS control.
Material engineering is a helpful approach for managing RCS.
Frequency Selective Surfaces (FSS) and metamaterials can be used for passive and adaptive RCS control.
Active and reconfigurable approaches can be used for RCS control.
Contemporary computational electromagnetic (CEM) software can provide sophisticated simulation environments to investigate electromagnetic scattering behavior.
Numerical simulations can help designers to test different setups, visualize current distributions, and predict scattering patterns before physical fabrication.
The baseline rectangular microstrip antenna has a resonant frequency of 3.9 GHz and a -10 dB bandwidth of 3.1-4.8 GHz.
Geometric modifications can improve the S11 response and increase the -10 dB bandwidth.
The hybrid antenna (Model C) has a -10 dB bandwidth of 3.5-7.8 GHz and achieves a maximum RCS reduction of up to 80% with a minimum value of -15 dBsm.
CST Microwave Studio (MWS) was used for simulation and modeling.
This study enhances the expanding field of low-observable antenna design, offering insights important for radar, aerospace, and communication systems where stealth performance is essential.
